pairs.video_summary: This video provides a comprehensive overview of basic machine learning concepts in just 22 minutes. It starts by differentiating artificial intelligence from machine learning, explaining that while AI mimics human tasks, not all AI involves learning from data. Key topics include supervised learning, where models learn from labeled data, and unsupervised learning, which identifies patterns without labels. It also covers reinforcement learning, emphasizing its trial-and-error approach. The video explains essential terms like algorithms, models, features, and the importance of training and test data. It discusses model complexity, bias-variance trade-off, and techniques like regularization and cross-validation to prevent overfitting. Finally, it touches on optimization methods like gradient descent and the significance of hyperparameters in training models.

pairs.paper_abstract:
this work explores the feasibility of steering a drone with a ( recurrent ) neural network , based on input from a forward looking camera , in the context of a high - level navigation task . 
 we set up a generic framework for training a network to perform navigation tasks based on imitation learning . 
 it can be applied to both aerial and land vehicles . as a proof of concept 
 we apply it to a uav ( unmanned aerial vehicle ) in a simulated environment , learning to cross a room containing a number of obstacles . 
 so far only feedforward neural networks ( fnns ) have been used to train uav control . to cope with more complex tasks , 
 we propose the use of recurrent neural networks ( rnn ) instead and successfully train an lstm ( long - short term memory ) network for controlling uavs . 
 vision based control is a sequential prediction problem , known for its highly correlated input data . 
 the correlation makes training a network hard , especially an rnn . to overcome this issue 
 , we investigate an alternative sampling method during training , namely window - wise truncated backpropagation through time ( ww - tbptt ) . 
 further , end - to - end training requires a lot of data which often is not available . 
 therefore , we compare the performance of retraining only the fully connected ( fc ) and lstm control layers with networks which are trained end - to - end . performing 
 the relatively simple task of crossing a room already reveals important guidelines and good practices for training neural control networks . 
 different visualizations help to explain the behavior learned .
pairs.paper_summary: this work explores the feasibility of steering a drone with a ( recurrent ) neural network , based on input from a forward looking camera , in the context of a high - level navigation task . we set up a generic framework for training a network to perform navigation tasks based on imitation learning .
pairs.video_summary:
The video features Nishal, a PhD student from Carnegie Mellon University, discussing her research on enhancing autonomous driving systems using graph neural networks (GNNs). She begins by outlining the standard perception and prediction pipeline in autonomous driving, which includes 3D object detection, tracking, and trajectory forecasting. Nishal explains how GNNs can improve interaction modeling in multi-object tracking and extend to tasks like object detection and data forecasting.

She highlights the importance of sensor data, particularly LiDAR, for accurate 3D localization, and discusses recent advancements in trajectory forecasting that account for multiple possible future paths. The video also covers the shift from traditional methods like Kalman filters to more complex deep learning approaches for tracking and forecasting. Nishal emphasizes the need for integrating perception and prediction modules for better performance and efficiency in autonomous systems. She concludes by sharing insights on optimizing the entire driving pipeline and the potential for future research in this area.

pairs.paper_abstract:
learning an algorithm from examples is a fundamental problem that has been widely studied . 
 it has been addressed using neural networks too , in particular by neural turing machines ( ntms ) . 
 these are fully differentiable computers that use backpropagation to learn their own programming . 
 despite their appeal ntms have a weakness that is caused by their sequential nature : they are not parallel and are are hard to train due to their large depth when unfolded . 
 we present a neural network architecture to address this problem : the _ neural gpu_. it is based on a type of convolutional gated recurrent unit and , like the ntm , is computationally universal . unlike the ntm , 
 the neural gpu is highly parallel which makes it easier to train and efficient to run . 
 an essential property of algorithms is their ability to handle inputs of arbitrary size . 
 we show that the neural gpu can be trained on short instances of an algorithmic task and successfully generalize to long instances . 
 we verified it on a number of tasks including long addition and long multiplication of numbers represented in binary . 
 we train the neural gpu on numbers with up - to @xmath0 bits and observe no errors whatsoever while testing it , even on much longer numbers .    to achieve these results we introduce a technique for training deep recurrent networks : parameter sharing relaxation . 
 we also found a small amount of dropout and gradient noise to have a large positive effect on learning and generalization .
pairs.paper_summary: learning an algorithm from examples is a fundamental problem that has been widely studied . it has been addressed using neural networks too , in particular by neural turing machines ( ntms ) . these are fully differentiable computers that use backpropagation to learn their own programming .
pairs.video_summary: The video dives into backpropagation, a key concept in training neural networks. It starts by explaining the structure of a simple neural network and the importance of calculating weights and biases for accurate predictions. The presenter outlines the gradient descent technique, emphasizing how to minimize the error function by adjusting these weights based on their gradients. A significant focus is on using the chain rule to compute these gradients efficiently, starting from the output layer and working backward through the network. The video also introduces the error function and its components, providing a clear, step-by-step approach to understanding how changes in weights affect overall performance.

pairs.paper_abstract:
in recent years , consumer unmanned aerial vehicles have become very popular , everyone can buy and fly a drone without previous experience , which raises concern in regards to regulations and public safety . in this paper , we present a novel approach towards enabling safe operation of such vehicles in urban areas . 
 our method uses geodetically accurate dataset images with geographical information system ( gis ) data of road networks and buildings provided by google maps , to compute a weighted a * shortest path from start to end locations of a mission . 
 weights represent the potential risk of injuries for individuals in all categories of land - use , i.e. flying over buildings is considered safer than above roads . 
 we enable safe uav operation in regards to 1- land - use by computing a static global path dependent on environmental structures , and 2- avoiding flying over moving objects such as cars and pedestrians by dynamically optimizing the path locally during the flight . 
 as all input sources are first geo - registered , pixels and gps coordinates are equivalent , it therefore allows us to generate an automated and user - friendly mission with gps waypoints readable by consumer drones autopilots . 
 we simulated 54 missions and show significant improvement in maximizing uav s standoff distance to moving objects with a quantified safety parameter over 40 times better than the naive straight line navigation .
pairs.paper_summary: in recent years , consumer unmanned aerial vehicles have become very popular , everyone can buy and fly a drone without previous experience , which raises concern in regards to regulations and public safety . in this paper , we present a novel approach towards enabling safe operation of such vehicles in urban areas .
pairs.video_summary: The video dives into the complexities of self-driving cars, emphasizing the challenges of localization and mapping. It discusses the limitations of current perception systems, particularly in adverse conditions like poor lighting and weather, and highlights the importance of robust algorithms for real-time navigation. The speaker shares insights from their experience with DARPA challenges, detailing how their vehicle used laser scanners and cameras for mapping and decision-making without relying solely on GPS. Additionally, the video touches on the evolution of autonomous systems, contrasting Google's approach with Tesla's, and introduces concepts from robotics like SLAM (Simultaneous Localization and Mapping) and the integration of object-based representations to enhance perception and navigation.

pairs.paper_abstract:
we study supervised learning and generalisation in coupled perceptrons trained on - line using two learning scenarios . in the first scenario 
 the teacher and the student are independent networks and both are represented by an ashkin - teller perceptron . in the second scenario the student and the teacher are simple perceptrons but are coupled by an ashkin - teller type four - neuron interaction term . 
 expressions for the generalisation error and the learning curves are derived for various learning algorithms . 
 the analytic results find excellent confirmation in numerical simulations .
pairs.paper_summary: we study supervised learning and generalisation in coupled perceptrons trained on - line using two learning scenarios . in the first scenario the teacher and the student are independent networks and both are represented by an ashkin - teller perceptron .
pairs.video_summary:
The video dives into the feasibility of learning in machine learning, starting with the essential criteria for applying machine learning: the existence of a pattern, the inability to mathematically define that pattern, and the necessity of having data. It emphasizes that while you can attempt learning without a clear pattern, having data is non-negotiable. The lecture then transitions into supervised learning, introducing the concept of a target function and the distinction between in-sample and out-of-sample performance, denoted as \(E_{in}(H)\) and \(E_{out}(H)\), respectively.

The presenter discusses the perceptron algorithm as a learning model, explaining how it adjusts hypotheses based on data. A significant portion of the lecture focuses on the Hoeffding inequality, which provides a probabilistic guarantee that in-sample performance can reflect out-of-sample performance, especially when dealing with multiple hypotheses. The discussion culminates in addressing the challenges of generalization and the need for a modified Hoeffding inequality to handle multiple hypotheses simultaneously, ensuring that learning is feasible in a broader context.

pairs.paper_abstract:
many day - to - day activities require the dexterous manipulation of a redundant humanoid arm in complex 3d environments . 
 however , position regulation of such robot arm systems becomes very difficult in presence of non - linear uncertainties in the system . 
 also , perturbations exist due to various unwanted interactions with obstacles for clumsy environments in which obstacle avoidance is not possible , and this makes position regulation even more difficult . 
 this report proposes a non - linear task - space disturbance observer by virtue of which position regulation of such robotic systems can be achieved in spite of such perturbations and uncertainties . 
 simulations are conducted using a 7-dof redundant robot arm system to show the effectiveness of the proposed method . 
 these results are then compared with the case of a conventional mass - damper based task - space disturbance observer to show the enhancement in performance using the developed concept . 
 this proposed method is then applied to a controller which exhibits human - like motion characteristics for reaching a target . 
 arbitrary perturbations in the form of interactions with obstacles are introduced in its path . 
 results show that the robot end - effector successfully continues to move in its path of a human - like quasi - straight trajectory even if the joint trajectories deviated by a considerable amount due to the perturbations . 
 these results are also compared with that of the unperturbed motion of the robot which further prove the significance of the developed scheme .
pairs.paper_summary: many day - to - day activities require the dexterous manipulation of a redundant humanoid arm in complex 3d environments . however , position regulation of such robot arm systems becomes very difficult in presence of non - linear uncertainties in the system .
pairs.video_summary: The video lecture on robotics covers the fundamentals of kinematics and dynamics in robotic systems. It starts with an explanation of forward and inverse kinematics, detailing how forward kinematics uses joint angles to determine the end effector's position, while inverse kinematics does the reverse. The Denavit-Hartenberg parameters are introduced for modeling these transformations. The lecture then transitions to dynamics, explaining the difference between forward dynamics (calculating motion from torque inputs) and inverse dynamics (determining required torques from desired motion). It also touches on control strategies, including a partition control law and the role of the Jacobian matrix in relating joint velocities to end effector velocities. Overall, it provides a comprehensive overview of robotic motion analysis and control techniques.

pairs.paper_abstract:
today s small and medium - sized enterprises ( smes ) in the software industry are faced with major challenges . while having to work efficiently using limited resources they have to perform quality assurance on their code to avoid the risk of further effort for bug fixes or compensations . 
 automated static analysis can reduce this risk because it promises little effort for running an analysis . 
 we report on our experience in analysing five projects from and with smes by three different static analysis techniques : code clone detection , bug pattern detection and architecture conformance analysis . 
 we found that the effort that was needed to introduce those techniques was small ( mostly below one person - hour ) , that we can detect diverse defects in production code and that the participating companies perceived the usefulness of the presented techniques as well as our analysis results high enough to include the techniques in their quality assurance .
pairs.paper_summary: today s small and medium - sized enterprises ( smes ) in the software industry are faced with major challenges . while having to work efficiently using limited resources they have to perform quality assurance on their code to avoid the risk of further effort for bug fixes or compensations .
pairs.video_summary: The video provides a comprehensive overview of software testing fundamentals, starting with unit tests and expanding into various testing types. It emphasizes that tests can't guarantee program correctness, referencing Edsger Dijkstra's insights. The presenter introduces Hoare logic, explaining the concept of the "Tony triple" to describe how code execution changes state. Different testing approaches are discussed, including dynamic testing (like unit tests), static testing (code reviews), and passive testing (monitoring side effects). Mutation testing is highlighted as a method to check the robustness of tests by introducing minor code changes. Finally, the video touches on property-based testing, demonstrating how it can validate properties across a range of inputs, enhancing test coverage and robustness.

pairs.paper_abstract:
this paper presents a new method for pre - training neural networks that can decrease the total training time for a neural network while maintaining the final performance , which motivates its use on deep neural networks . by partitioning the training task in multiple training subtasks with sub - models , which can be performed independently and in parallel 
 , it is shown that the size of the sub - models reduces almost quadratically with the number of subtasks created , quickly scaling down the sub - models used for the pre - training . 
 the sub - models are then merged to provide a pre - trained initial set of weights for the original model . 
 the proposed method is independent of the other aspects of the training , such as architecture of the neural network , training method , and objective , making it compatible with a wide range of existing approaches . 
 the speedup without loss of performance is validated experimentally on mnist and on cifar10 data sets , also showing that even performing the subtasks sequentially can decrease the training time . 
 moreover , we show that larger models may present higher speedups and conjecture about the benefits of the method in distributed learning systems .
pairs.paper_summary: this paper presents a new method for pre - training neural networks that can decrease the total training time for a neural network while maintaining the final performance , which motivates its use on deep neural networks .
pairs.video_summary: The video explains the fundamentals of neural networks, which are essential for deep learning. It covers the structure of a neural network, including input, hidden, and output layers, and details how data is processed through forward propagation and backpropagation. The training process is highlighted, where the network adjusts weights based on prediction errors, and it discusses practical applications like facial recognition, forecasting, and music composition.

pairs.paper_abstract:
state - of - the - art algorithms for semantic visual tasks  such as image classification and semantic segmentation  are based on the use of convolutional neural networks . 
 these networks are commonly trained , and evaluated , on large annotated datasets of high - quality images that are free of artifacts . in this paper , we investigate the effect of one such artifact that is quite common in natural capture settings  blur . 
 we show that standard pre - trained network models suffer a significant degradation in performance when applied to blurred images . 
 we investigate the extent to which this degradation is due to the mismatch between training and input image statistics . 
 specifically , we find that fine - tuning a pre - trained model with blurred images added to the training set allows it to regain much of the lost accuracy . by considering different combinations of sharp and blurred images in the training set , 
 we characterize how much degradation is caused by loss of information , and how much by the uncertainty of not knowing the nature and magnitude of blur . 
 we find that by fine - tuning on a diverse mix of blurred images , convolutional neural networks can in fact learn to generate a blur invariant representation in their hidden layers . 
 broadly , our results provide practitioners with useful insights for developing vision systems that perform reliably on real world images affected by blur .
pairs.paper_summary: state - of - the - art algorithms for semantic visual tasks such as image classification and semantic segmentation are based on the use of convolutional neural networks . these networks are commonly trained , and evaluated , on large annotated datasets of high - quality images that are free of artifacts .
pairs.video_summary:
In this lecture on traditional computer vision, the focus is on understanding convolution operations and classical filters. The instructor explains how filters, which are essentially matrices (like 3x3 or 5x5), are used to capture features in images, such as edges and corners. Key filters discussed include the Sobel filter, Laplacian filter, and Prewitt filter, each designed for specific tasks like edge detection or smoothing. The lecture details how convolution works by moving these filters across an image, performing element-wise multiplication, and summing the results to produce a new intensity value for the output image.

The instructor emphasizes the importance of these traditional techniques as foundational knowledge for understanding modern deep learning approaches, where filters are learned rather than handcrafted. Practical examples illustrate how filters can enhance image features and suppress noise. The lecture concludes with a demonstration of filters in convolutional neural networks, reinforcing their relevance in both classical and contemporary computer vision applications.

pairs.paper_abstract:
the graph laplacian , a typical representation of a network , is an important matrix that can tell us much about the network structure . in particular its eigenpairs ( eigenvalues and eigenvectors ) 
 incubate precious topological information about the network at hand , including connectivity , partitioning , node distance and centrality . 
 real networks might be very large in number of nodes ( actors ) ; luckily , most real networks are sparse , meaning that the number of edges ( binary connections among actors ) are few with respect to the maximum number of possible edges . in this paper 
 we experimentally compare three state - of - the - art algorithms for computation of a few among the smallest eigenpairs of large and sparse matrices : the implicitly restarted lanczos method , which is the current implementation in the most popular scientific computing environments ( matlab @xmath0 r ) , the jacobi - davidson method , and the deflation accelerated conjugate gradient method . 
 we implemented the algorithms in a uniform programming setting and tested them over diverse real - world networks including biological , technological , information , and social networks . 
 it turns out that the jacobi - davidson method displays the best performance in terms of number of matrix - vector products and cpu time . 
 graph laplacian ; eigenpair computation ; algorithms ; networks .
pairs.paper_summary: the graph laplacian , a typical representation of a network , is an important matrix that can tell us much about the network structure . in particular its eigenpairs ( eigenvalues and eigenvectors ) incubate precious topological information about the network at hand , including connectivity , partitioning , node distance and centrality .
pairs.video_summary: The video dives into combinatorial optimization on graphs and the role of graph neural networks (GNNs). It starts by contrasting convolutional neural networks' success in image processing with the challenges of applying similar techniques to graph data, emphasizing the need for permutation invariance in GNNs. The speaker discusses various types of GNNs, including spectral GNNs and message-passing networks, and their applications in fields like computational chemistry and social network analysis. Specific examples include using GNNs for classifying communities in stochastic block models and solving the max cut and quadratic assignment problems. The video also touches on open problems in GNN research, such as improving expressiveness and scalability while maintaining invariance.

pairs.paper_abstract:
this paper presents a systematic evaluation of neural network ( nn ) for classification of real - world data . in the field of machine learning 
 , it is often seen that a single parameter that is ` predictive accuracy ' is being used for evaluating the performance of a classifier model . 
 however , this parameter might not be considered reliable given a dataset with very high level of skewness . to demonstrate such behavior , 
 seven different types of datasets have been used to evaluate a multilayer perceptron ( mlp ) using twelve(12 ) different parameters which include micro- and macro - level estimation . in the present study , 
 the most common problem of prediction called ` multiclass ' classification has been considered . 
 the results that are obtained for different parameters for each of the dataset could demonstrate interesting findings to support the usability of these set of performance evaluation parameters .
pairs.paper_summary: this paper presents a systematic evaluation of neural network ( nn ) for classification of real - world data . in the field of machine learning , it is often seen that a single parameter that is ` predictive accuracy ' is being used for evaluating the performance of a classifier model .
pairs.video_summary: The video introduces the basics of machine learning, emphasizing different paradigms like supervised, unsupervised, and reinforcement learning. It starts with a definition of machine learning, highlighting the importance of defining tasks, performance measures, and experience for effective learning. Supervised learning is explained as mapping inputs to outputs, with classification and regression as key tasks. Unsupervised learning focuses on discovering patterns in data, with clustering and association rule mining as examples. The video also touches on challenges in building machine learning models, such as model selection, data quality, and performance evaluation, setting the stage for deeper exploration in subsequent lectures.

pairs.paper_abstract:
Attentional, RNN-based encoder-decoder models for abstractive summarization
have achieved good performance on short input and output sequences. For longer
documents and summaries however these models often include repetitive and
incoherent phrases. We introduce a neural network model with a novel
intra-attention that attends over the input and continuously generated output
separately, and a new training method that combines standard supervised word
prediction and reinforcement learning (RL). Models trained only with supervised
learning often exhibit "exposure bias" - they assume ground truth is provided
at each step during training. However, when standard word prediction is
combined with the global sequence prediction training of RL the resulting
summaries become more readable. We evaluate this model on the CNN/Daily Mail
and New York Times datasets. Our model obtains a 41.16 ROUGE-1 score on the
CNN/Daily Mail dataset, an improvement over previous state-of-the-art models.
Human evaluation also shows that our model produces higher quality summaries.
pairs.paper_summary: Attentional, RNN-based encoder-decoder models for abstractive summarization have achieved good performance on short input and output sequences. For longer documents and summaries however these models often include repetitive and incoherent phrases.
pairs.video_summary: The video dives into the attention mechanism, explaining its role in improving machine translation by addressing the limitations of RNNs. It details how the encoder and decoder work together, with the encoder creating a universal meaning representation and the decoder generating translations based on attention scores. The presenter illustrates how similarity scores between decoder and encoder states are computed using dot products and transformed into a probability distribution with the softmax function, ultimately leading to the creation of an attention vector that enhances translation accuracy.

pairs.paper_abstract:
deep neural networks have greatly improved the performance of various applications including image processing , speech recognition , natural language processing , and bioinformatics . 
 however , it is still difficult to discover or interpret knowledge from the inference provided by a deep neural network , since its internal representation has many nonlinear and complex parameters embedded in hierarchical layers . 
 therefore , it becomes important to establish a new methodology by which deep neural networks can be understood .    in this paper 
 , we propose a new method for extracting a global and simplified structure from a layered neural network . based on network analysis 
 , the proposed method detects communities or clusters of units with similar connection patterns . 
 we show its effectiveness by applying it to three use cases . 
 ( 1 ) network decomposition : it can decompose a trained neural network into multiple small independent networks thus dividing the problem and reducing the computation time . 
 ( 2 ) training assessment : the appropriateness of a trained result with a given hyperparameter or randomly chosen initial parameters can be evaluated by using a modularity index . and ( 3 ) data analysis : in practical data it reveals the community structure in the input , hidden , and output layers , which serves as a clue for discovering knowledge from a trained neural network . 
 + _ keywords _ : layered neural networks , network analysis , community detection
pairs.paper_summary: deep neural networks have greatly improved the performance of various applications including image processing , speech recognition , natural language processing , and bioinformatics . however , it is still difficult to discover or interpret knowledge from the inference provided by a deep neural network , since its internal representation has many nonlinear and complex parameters embedded in hierarchical layers .
pairs.video_summary: The video dives into combinatorial optimization on graphs and the role of graph neural networks (GNNs). It starts by contrasting convolutional neural networks' success in image processing with the challenges of applying similar techniques to graph data, emphasizing the need for permutation invariance in GNNs. The speaker discusses various types of GNNs, including spectral GNNs and message-passing networks, and their applications in fields like computational chemistry and social network analysis. Specific examples include using GNNs for classifying communities in stochastic block models and solving the max cut and quadratic assignment problems. The video also touches on open problems in GNN research, such as improving expressiveness and scalability while maintaining invariance.

pairs.paper_abstract:
designing appropriate features for acoustic event recognition tasks is an active field of research . 
 expressive features should both improve the performance of the tasks and also be interpret - able . 
 currently , heuristically designed features based on the domain knowledge requires tremendous effort in hand - crafting , while features extracted through deep network are difficult for human to interpret . in this work 
 , we explore the experience guided learning method for designing acoustic features . 
 this is a novel hybrid approach combining both domain knowledge and purely data driven feature designing . 
 based on the procedure of log mel - filter banks , we design a filter bank learning layer . 
 we concatenate this layer with a convolutional neural network ( cnn ) model . after training the network , 
 the weight of the filter bank learning layer is extracted to facilitate the design of acoustic features . 
 we smooth the trained weight of the learning layer and re - initialize it in filter bank learning layer as audio feature extractor . for the environmental sound recognition task based on the _ urbansound8k _ dataset  @xcite , 
 the experience guided learning leads to a 2% accuracy improvement compared with the fixed feature extractors ( the log mel - filter bank ) . 
 the shape of the new filter banks are visualized and explained to prove the effectiveness of the feature design process . 
 filter bank , feature learning , experience guide learning , data driven , neural network
pairs.paper_summary: designing appropriate features for acoustic event recognition tasks is an active field of research . expressive features should both improve the performance of the tasks and also be interpret - able . currently , heuristically designed features based on the domain knowledge requires tremendous effort in hand - crafting , while features extracted through deep network are difficult for human to interpret .
pairs.video_summary: The video explains the fundamentals of neural networks, which are essential for deep learning. It covers the structure of a neural network, including input, hidden, and output layers, and details how data is processed through forward propagation and backpropagation. The training process is highlighted, where the network adjusts weights based on prediction errors, and it discusses practical applications like facial recognition, forecasting, and music composition.

pairs.paper_abstract:
in computational biology , biological entities such as genes or proteins are usually annotated with terms extracted from gene ontology ( go ) . the functional similarity among terms of an ontology 
 is evaluated by using semantic similarity measures ( ssm ) . 
 more recently , the extensive application of ssms yielded to the semantic similarity networks ( ssns ) . 
 ssns are edge - weighted graphs where the nodes are concepts ( e.g. proteins ) and each edge has an associated weight that represents the semantic similarity among related pairs of nodes . 
 the analysis of ssns may reveal biologically meaningful knowledge . for these aims , 
 the need for the introduction of tool able to manage and analyze ssn arises . 
 consequently we developed ssn - analyzer a web based tool able to build and preprocess ssn . 
 as proof of concept we demonstrate that community detection algorithms applied to filtered ( thresholded ) networks , have better performances in terms of biological relevance of the results , with respect to the use of raw unfiltered networks .
pairs.paper_summary: in computational biology , biological entities such as genes or proteins are usually annotated with terms extracted from gene ontology ( go ) . the functional similarity among terms of an ontology is evaluated by using semantic similarity measures ( ssm ) . more recently , the extensive application of ssms yielded to the semantic similarity networks ( ssns ) .
pairs.video_summary: The video introduces graph neural networks (GNNs) and their application in discovering new antibiotics like halicin. It explains how GNNs differ from traditional neural networks by effectively handling unstructured data represented as graphs, where nodes symbolize entities and edges represent relationships. The presenter details the message-passing mechanism, where nodes aggregate information from their neighbors to create node embeddings, and discusses various tasks like link prediction, node classification, and clustering, emphasizing the importance of learning good embeddings through backpropagation and different aggregation methods.

pairs.paper_abstract:
the brazilian government often misclassifies the goods it buys . 
 that makes it hard to audit government expenditures . 
 we can not know whether the price paid for a ballpoint pen ( code # 7510 ) was reasonable if the pen was misclassified as a technical drawing pen ( code # 6675 ) or as any other good . 
 this paper shows how we can use machine learning to reduce misclassification . 
 i trained a support vector machine ( svm ) classifier that takes a product description as input and returns the most likely category codes as output . 
 i trained the classifier using 20 million goods purchased by the brazilian government between 1999 - 04 - 01 and 2015 - 04 - 02 . in 83.3% of the cases the correct category code was one of the three most likely category codes identified by the classifier . 
 i used the trained classifier to develop a web app that might help the government reduce misclassification . 
 i open sourced the code on github ; anyone can use and modify it .
pairs.paper_summary: the brazilian government often misclassifies the goods it buys . that makes it hard to audit government expenditures . we can not know whether the price paid for a ballpoint pen ( code # 7510 ) was reasonable if the pen was misclassified as a technical drawing pen ( code # 6675 ) or as any other good .
pairs.video_summary: The video introduces support vector machines (SVMs) in an intuitive way, using a scenario of predicting medical school admissions based on GPA and MCAT scores. It explains the concept of the decision boundary and how SVMs aim to maximize the margin between classes, highlighting the importance of support vectors in defining this margin. The video also contrasts hard margin SVMs, which require clear class separation, with soft margin SVMs, which allow for some misclassifications and apply penalties, making them more practical for real-world data.

pairs.paper_abstract:
the robocup 2d simulation league incorporates several challenging features , setting a benchmark for artificial intelligence ( ai ) . in this paper 
 we describe some of the ideas and tools around the development of our team , gliders2012 . in our description , we focus on the evaluation function as one of our central mechanisms for action selection 
 . we also point to a new framework for watching log files in a web browser that we release for use and further development by the robocup community . 
 finally , we also summarize results of the group and final matches we played during robocup 2012 , with gliders2012 finishing 4th out of 19 teams .
pairs.paper_summary: the robocup 2d simulation league incorporates several challenging features , setting a benchmark for artificial intelligence ( ai ) . in this paper we describe some of the ideas and tools around the development of our team , gliders2012 . in our description , we focus on the evaluation function as one of our central mechanisms for action selection .
pairs.video_summary: The video starts by transitioning into the second module of the Artificial Intelligence course, focusing on state space search. It begins with a recap of key concepts from the previous module, including definitions of intelligence and rational agents. The lecture then dives into the formulation of search problems, explaining how to represent states, actions, and goals. It introduces the concept of a state space, where each state represents a configuration of the agent's environment. The instructor discusses various search strategies, such as depth-first and breadth-first search, and highlights the importance of problem formulation. Examples like the eight queens problem and the Mars rover are used to illustrate state space representation and the evaluation of agent performance. The session concludes with a challenge for viewers to formulate their own state space problems.

pairs.paper_abstract:
the availability of infrastructure - as - a - service ( iaas ) computing clouds gives researchers access to a large set of new resources for running complex scientific applications . 
 however , exploiting cloud resources for large numbers of jobs requires significant effort and expertise . in order to make it simple and transparent for researchers to deploy their applications , 
 we have developed a virtual machine resource manager ( ) for distributed compute clouds . 
 boots and manages the user - customized virtual machines in response to a user s job submission . 
 we describe the motivation and design of the and present results on its use on both science and commercial clouds .    * cloud scheduler : a resource manager for distributed compute clouds *    p. armstrong@xmath0 , a. agarwal@xmath0 , a. bishop@xmath0 , a. charbonneau@xmath1 , r. desmarais@xmath0 , k. fransham@xmath0 , n. hill@xmath2 , i. gable@xmath0 , s. gaudet@xmath2 , s. goliath@xmath2 , r. impey@xmath1 , c. leavett - brown@xmath0 , j. ouellete@xmath2 , m. paterson@xmath0 , c. pritchet@xmath0 , d. penfold - brown@xmath0 , w. podaima@xmath1 , d. schade@xmath2 , r.j . 
 sobie@xmath3    @xmath0 department of physics and astronomy , university of victoria , victoria , canada v8w 3p6 + @xmath1 national research council canada , 100 sussex drive , ottawa , canada + @xmath2 national research council herzberg institute of astrophysics , 5071 west saanich road , victoria , bc , canada , v9e 3e7 + @xmath4 institute of particle physics of canada .
pairs.paper_summary: the availability of infrastructure - as - a - service ( iaas ) computing clouds gives researchers access to a large set of new resources for running complex scientific applications . however , exploiting cloud resources for large numbers of jobs requires significant effort and expertise .
pairs.video_summary: The video outlines a roadmap for building a career in cloud computing, especially for those not inclined towards programming. It emphasizes the importance of strong fundamentals in networking, operating systems (particularly Linux), virtualization, and databases. The speaker suggests starting with a major cloud provider like AWS or Azure, utilizing their free tiers for hands-on experience, and pursuing certifications to enhance job prospects. It also touches on potential career paths and salary expectations in the field.

pairs.paper_abstract:
we propose the object - oriented networking ( oon ) framework , for meeting the generalized interconnection , mobility and technology integration requirements underlining the internet . in oon , 
 the various objects that need to be accessed through the internet ( content , smart things , services , people , etc . ) are viewed as network layer resources , rather than as application layer resources as in the ip communications model . by abstracting them as computing objects -with attributes and methods- 
 they are identified by expressive , discoverable names , while data are exchanged between them in the context of their methods , based on suitably defined system - specific names . 
 an oon - enabled internet is not only a global data delivery medium but also a universal object discovery and service development platform ; service - level interactions can be realized through native network means , without requiring standardized protocols . 
 oon can be realized through existing software - defined networking or network functions virtualization technologies and it can be deployed in an incremental fashion . 
 internet architecture , information - centric networks , object - oriented programming , routing , ioe , iot .

pairs.video_summary: The video dives into the fundamentals of logical and IP addressing, explaining the differences between IPv4 and IPv6. It highlights that IPv4 uses a 32-bit address, allowing for over 4 billion combinations, while IPv6 expands this to 128 bits, accommodating the growing number of devices needing unique addresses. The presenter discusses the concepts of uniqueness and universality in IP addresses, likening them to passports for global identification. It also covers binary and dotted decimal notations for IP representation, and introduces classful addressing, detailing how addresses are divided into classes A, B, and C based on network size and requirements. The video sets the stage for more advanced topics like subnetting and classless inter-domain routing in future discussions.

machine - learning algorithms offer immense possibilities in the development of several cognitive applications .

 . however , the network complexities of large - scale classifiers present them as one of the most challenging and energy intensive workloads across the computing spectrum . in this paper , we present a new approach to optimize energy efficiency of object detection tasks using semantic decomposition to build a hierarchical classification framework . 
 we observe that certain semantic information like color / texture are common across various images in real - world datasets for object detection applications . 
 we exploit these common semantic features to distinguish the objects of interest from the remaining inputs ( non - objects of interest ) in a dataset at a lower computational effort . 
 we propose a 2-stage hierarchical classification framework , with increasing levels of complexity , wherein the first stage is trained to recognize the broad representative semantic features relevant to the object of interest . 
 the first stage rejects the input instances that do not have the representative features and passes only the relevant instances to the second stage . 
 our methodology thus allows us to reject certain information at lower complexity and utilize the full computational effort of a network only on a smaller fraction of inputs to perform detection . 
 we use color and texture as distinctive traits to carry out several experiments for object detection . 
 our experiments on the caltech101/cifar10 dataset show that the proposed method yields 1.93x/1.46x improvement in average energy , respectively , over the traditional single classifier model .

It highlights the YOLO (You Only Look Once) method, which significantly speeds up detection by processing images in a single pass rather than evaluating multiple regions. The speaker also discusses real-time applications, including self-driving cars and medical imaging, and emphasizes the accessibility of their open-source framework, Darknet, which allows anyone to leverage these powerful detection capabilities.

pairs.video_summary:
The video features an interview with Jensen Huang, CEO of NVIDIA, discussing the evolution of computing and the future of robotics and AI. He highlights the pivotal role of GPUs in transforming computing, particularly through parallel processing, which allows for simultaneous calculations. This shift began in the 90s with the development of the first modern GPU, driven by the need for better graphics in video games. Huang explains how CUDA, a programming platform for GPUs, democratized access to this computing power, enabling breakthroughs in AI, such as the success of AlexNet in image recognition.

He also introduces NVIDIA's Omniverse and Cosmos, tools for training robots in simulated environments, allowing them to learn faster and more safely than traditional methods. Huang envisions a future where robotics is ubiquitous, with every moving object being robotic, and emphasizes the importance of AI in enhancing human capabilities. He concludes by encouraging viewers to embrace AI as a tool for empowerment in various fields, underscoring the optimistic potential of technology to shape our future.

pairs.paper_abstract:
we propose a novel foundational framework for _ why - not explanations _ , 
 that is , explanations for why a tuple is missing from a query result . 
 our why - not explanations leverage concepts from an ontology to provide high - level and meaningful reasons for why a tuple is missing from the result of a query . 
 a key algorithmic problem in our framework is that of _ computing a most - general explanation _ for a why - not question , relative to an ontology , which can either be provided by the user , or it may be automatically derived from the data and/or schema . 
 we study the complexity of this problem and associated problems , and present concrete algorithms for computing why - not explanations . in the case where an external ontology is provided , 
 we first show that the problem of deciding the existence of an explanation to a why - not question is np - complete in general . however , the problem is solvable in polynomial time for queries of bounded arity , provided that the ontology is specified in a suitable language , such as a member of the dl - lite family of description logics , which allows for efficient concept subsumption checking . 
 furthermore , we show that a most - general explanation can be computed in polynomial time in this case . in addition , we propose a method for deriving a suitable ( virtual ) ontology from a database and/or a schema , and we present an algorithm for computing a most - general explanation to a why - not question , relative to such ontologies . 
 this algorithm runs in polynomial - time in the case when concepts are defined in a selection - free language , or if the underlying schema is fixed . 
 finally , we also study the problem of computing _ short _ most - general explanations , and we briefly discuss alternative definitions of what it means to be an explanation , and to be most general .

pairs.video_summary: The video dives into issues in knowledge representation, emphasizing its goal of facilitating conclusions from knowledge. It covers key topics like identifying important attributes (instance vs. is-a generalization), exploring relationships among attributes (like hierarchy and reasoning for values), and the significance of choosing granularity and object sets. It also discusses how to efficiently structure a knowledge base to retrieve relevant data, addressing challenges in finding appropriate information within a large dataset.

pairs.paper_abstract:
existing object proposal algorithms usually search for possible object regions over multiple locations and scales _ separately _ , which ignore the interdependency among different objects and deviate from the human perception procedure . 
 to incorporate global interdependency between objects into object localization , we propose an effective tree - structured reinforcement learning ( tree - rl ) approach to sequentially search for objects by fully exploiting both the current observation and historical search paths . 
 the tree - rl approach learns multiple searching policies through maximizing the long - term reward that reflects localization accuracies over all the objects . starting with taking the entire image as a proposal , the tree - rl approach allows the agent to sequentially discover multiple objects via a tree - structured traversing scheme . allowing multiple near - optimal policies , tree - rl offers more diversity in search paths and is able to find multiple objects with a single feed - forward pass . 
 therefore , tree - rl can better cover different objects with various scales which is quite appealing in the context of object proposal . 
 experiments on pascal voc 2007 and 2012 validate the effectiveness of the tree - rl , which can achieve comparable recalls with current object proposal algorithms via much fewer candidate windows .

pairs.video_summary: The video provides a comprehensive overview of the YOLO (You Only Look Once) algorithm used for object detection. It starts by explaining the differences between image classification, localization, and object detection, emphasizing that YOLO can detect multiple objects in a single image while providing bounding box coordinates. Balaji discusses how images are divided into grids, with each grid cell predicting the presence of objects and their bounding boxes. Key concepts like Intersection over Union (IoU) for evaluating bounding box accuracy, non-max suppression to eliminate duplicate detections, and anchor boxes for handling multiple objects in a grid cell are also covered. The video concludes with a summary of the output structure of YOLO and encourages viewers to explore further research for a deeper understanding.

pairs.paper_abstract:
this paper presents a simple , robust and ( almost ) unsupervised dictionary - based method , _ qwn - ppv _ ( q - wordnet as personalized pageranking vector ) to automatically generate polarity lexicons . 
 we show that _ qwn - ppv _ outperforms other automatically generated lexicons for the four extrinsic evaluations presented here . 
 it also shows very competitive and robust results with respect to manually annotated ones . 
 results suggest that no single lexicon is best for every task and dataset and that the intrinsic evaluation of polarity lexicons is not a good performance indicator on a sentiment analysis task . 
 the _ qwn - ppv _ method allows to easily create quality polarity lexicons whenever no domain - based annotated corpora are available for a given language .

pairs.video_summary: The video dives into using pre-trained word embeddings for sentiment analysis, specifically with an Amazon review dataset. It starts by reviewing word2vec and its two models, then transitions to how to implement sentiment classification using a bidirectional LSTM. The presenter explains data preparation steps, including tokenization, vocabulary building, and padding sequences to a uniform length. They detail the model architecture, emphasizing the bidirectional nature of LSTMs to capture context from both directions in the text. The video also touches on training techniques, including fine-tuning pre-trained embeddings and managing overfitting with early stopping, before concluding with how to predict sentiment from new reviews.

pairs.paper_abstract:
in comparison with document summarization on the articles from social media and newswire , argumentative zoning ( az ) is an important task in scientific paper analysis . traditional methodology to carry on 
 this task relies on feature engineering from different levels . in this paper , 
 three models of generating sentence vectors for the task of sentence classification were explored and compared . 
 the proposed approach builds sentence representations using learned embeddings based on neural network . 
 the learned word embeddings formed a feature space , to which the examined sentence is mapped to . 
 those features are input into the classifiers for supervised classification . using 10-cross - validation scheme ,

 the results showed that simply averaging the word vectors in a sentence works better than the paragraph to vector algorithm and by integrating specific cuewords into the loss function of the neural network can improve the classification performance . in comparison with the hand - crafted features , the word2vec method won for most of the categories . 
 however , the hand - crafted features showed their strength on classifying some of the categories .

pairs.video_summary: The video dives into Word2Vec, a natural language processing technique that converts words into vector representations. It starts by explaining the importance of transforming text into numerical data for machine learning, then introduces the concept of stop words and their removal. The main techniques discussed are the Skip-Gram model, which captures context by identifying neighboring words within a specified window size, and Negative Sampling, which introduces examples of words that aren't in close proximity to balance the training data. The presenter also clarifies the dual embedding approach in Word2Vec, distinguishing between main embeddings (which are retained) and context embeddings (used during training). Finally, it covers how the algorithm updates these vectors based on similarity scores derived from dot products and sigmoid functions, ultimately positioning similar words closer together in a high-dimensional space.

pairs.paper_abstract:
we derive a synaptic weight update rule for learning temporally precise spike train to spike train transformations in multilayer feedforward networks of spiking neurons . 
 the framework , aimed at seamlessly generalizing error backpropagation to the deterministic spiking neuron setting , is based strictly on spike timing and avoids invoking concepts pertaining to spike rates or probabilistic models of spiking . 
 the derivation is founded on two innovations . 
 first , an error functional is proposed that compares the spike train emitted by the output neuron of the network to the desired spike train by way of their putative impact on a virtual postsynaptic neuron . 
 this formulation sidesteps the need for spike alignment and leads to closed form solutions for all quantities of interest . 
 second , virtual assignment of weights to spikes rather than synapses enables a perturbation analysis of individual spike times and synaptic weights of the output as well as all intermediate neurons in the network , which yields the gradients of the error functional with respect to the said entities . learning proceeds via a gradient descent mechanism that leverages these quantities . 
 simulation experiments demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed learning framework 
 . the experiments also highlight asymmetries between synapses on excitatory and inhibitory neurons .

pairs.video_summary: The video dives into backpropagation in neural networks, explaining how it adjusts weights to minimize error between predicted and desired outputs. It starts with a forward pass to calculate outputs from input nodes through hidden layers, using specific formulas for activation and error calculation. Then, it details the backward pass, where it computes gradients using partial derivatives to update weights, ultimately demonstrating how repeated iterations can significantly reduce error, showcasing the practical application of backpropagation in machine learning.

pairs.paper_abstract:
image based reconstruction of urban environments is a challenging problem that deals with optimization of large number of variables , and has several sources of errors like the presence of dynamic objects . 
 since most large scale approaches make the assumption of observing static scenes , dynamic objects are relegated to the noise modeling section of such systems . 
 this is an approach of convenience since the ransac based framework used to compute most multiview geometric quantities for static scenes naturally confine dynamic objects to the class of outlier measurements . 
 however , reconstructing dynamic objects along with the static environment helps us get a complete picture of an urban environment . 
 such understanding can then be used for important robotic tasks like path planning for autonomous navigation , obstacle tracking and avoidance , and other areas .    in this paper 
 , we propose a system for robust slam that works in both static and dynamic environments . to overcome the challenge of dynamic objects in the scene 
 , we propose a new model to incorporate _ 
 semantic constraints _ into the reconstruction algorithm . while some of these constraints are based on multi - layered dense crfs trained over appearance _ as well as motion cues _ 
 , other proposed constraints can be expressed as additional terms in the bundle adjustment optimization process that does iterative refinement of 3d structure and camera / object motion trajectories . 
 we show results on the challenging kitti urban dataset for accuracy of motion segmentation and reconstruction of the trajectory and shape of moving objects relative to ground truth . 
 we are able to show average relative error reduction by a significant amount for moving object trajectory reconstruction relative to state - of - the - art methods like viso 2@xcite , as well as standard bundle adjustment algorithms .

pairs.video_summary: The video dives into the complexities of self-driving cars, emphasizing the challenges of localization and mapping. It discusses the limitations of current perception systems, particularly in adverse conditions like poor lighting and weather, and highlights the importance of robust algorithms for real-time navigation. The speaker shares insights from their experience with DARPA challenges, detailing how their vehicle used laser scanners and cameras for mapping and decision-making without relying solely on GPS. Additionally, the video touches on the evolution of autonomous systems, contrasting Google's approach with Tesla's, and introduces concepts from robotics like SLAM (Simultaneous Localization and Mapping) and the integration of object-based representations to enhance perception and navigation.

pairs.paper_abstract:
this paper presents evidence for the idea that much of artificial intelligence , human perception and cognition , mainstream computing , and mathematics , may be understood as compression of information via the matching and unification of patterns . 
 this is the basis for the _ sp theory of intelligence _ , outlined in the paper and fully described elsewhere . 
 relevant evidence may be seen : in empirical support for the sp theory ; in some advantages of information compression ( ic ) in terms of biology and engineering ; in our use of shorthands and ordinary words in language ; in how we merge successive views of any one thing ; in visual recognition ; in binocular vision ; in visual adaptation ; in how we learn lexical and grammatical structures in language ; and in perceptual constancies . 
 ic via the matching and unification of patterns may be seen in both computing and mathematics : in ic via equations ; in the matching and unification of names ; in the reduction or removal of redundancy from unary numbers ; in the workings of post s canonical system and the transition function in the universal turing machine ; in the way computers retrieve information from memory ; in systems like prolog ; and in the query - by - example technique for information retrieval . the chunking - with - codes technique for ic may be seen in the use of named functions to avoid repetition of computer code . 
 the schema - plus - correction technique may be seen in functions with parameters and in the use of classes in object - oriented programming . and the run - length coding technique may be seen in multiplication , in division , and in several other devices in mathematics and computing . 
 the sp theory resolves the apparent paradox of `` decompression by compression '' . and 
 computing and cognition as ic is compatible with the uses of redundancy in such things as backup copies to safeguard data and understanding speech in a noisy environment .

pairs.video_summary:
In this lecture, Adam introduces key concepts in cognitive science, focusing on artificial intelligence (AI), Turing machines, and neural networks. He distinguishes between weak (narrow) AI, which excels in specific tasks like chess or poker, and strong (general) AI, capable of performing a variety of tasks similar to humans. The discussion then shifts to Turing machines, explaining their structure and function as abstract models that manipulate symbols based on explicit rules, akin to human cognitive processes. 

Adam contrasts this with neural networks, emphasizing that they derive rules from large datasets rather than starting with predefined rules. He explains supervised learning using labeled data for tasks like image classification, and unsupervised learning, which identifies patterns in unlabeled data. The lecture concludes with a thought-provoking exploration of friendship types—pleasure, utility, and virtue—inviting reflection on how these concepts apply to relationships with AI and robots, and whether new categories of friendship might emerge as technology evolves.

pairs.paper_abstract:
Language model (LM) pre-training is useful in many language processing tasks.
But can pre-trained LMs be further leveraged for more general machine learning
problems? We propose an approach for using LMs to scaffold learning and
generalization in general sequential decision-making problems. In this
approach, goals and observations are represented as a sequence of embeddings,
and a policy network initialized with a pre-trained LM predicts the next
action. We demonstrate that this framework enables effective combinatorial
generalization across different environments and supervisory modalities. We
begin by assuming access to a set of expert demonstrations, and show that
initializing policies with LMs and fine-tuning them via behavior cloning
improves task completion rates by 43.6% in the VirtualHome environment. Next,
we integrate an active data gathering procedure in which agents iteratively
interact with the environment, relabel past "failed" experiences with new
goals, and update their policies in a self-supervised loop. Active data
gathering further improves combinatorial generalization, outperforming the best
baseline by 25.1%. Finally, we explain these results by investigating three
possible factors underlying the effectiveness of the LM-based policy. We find
that sequential input representations (vs. fixed-dimensional feature vectors)
and LM-based weight initialization are both important for generalization.
Surprisingly, however, the format of the policy inputs encoding (e.g. as a
natural language string vs. an arbitrary sequential encoding) has little
influence. Together, these results suggest that language modeling induces
representations that are useful for modeling not just language, but also goals
and plans; these representations can aid learning and generalization even
outside of language processing.
pairs.paper_summary: Language model (LM) pre-training is useful in many language processing tasks. But can pre-trained LMs be further leveraged for more general machine learning problems? We propose an approach for using LMs to scaffold learning and generalization in general sequential decision-making problems.
pairs.video_summary:
The video provides a comprehensive introduction to machine learning, starting with the fundamental concept of learning as the ability to improve behavior based on experience. It explains that machine learning is a subset of artificial intelligence focused on data and algorithms, emphasizing how machines can learn from past data to make predictions. The presenter outlines the main types of machine learning: supervised, unsupervised, and reinforcement learning. 

In supervised learning, labeled data is used for training, with examples like spam filtering. Unsupervised learning, on the other hand, involves clustering data without pre-assigned labels, allowing the algorithm to discover patterns independently. Reinforcement learning is described as a feedback-based approach where an agent learns from interactions with its environment.

The video also touches on various applications of machine learning, including image recognition, speech recognition, traffic prediction, product recommendations, and self-driving cars. It concludes with a brief history of machine learning milestones, such as the Turing Test and the introduction of deep learning. Overall, it serves as a solid foundation for understanding machine learning concepts and techniques.

It explains how YOLO processes images by dividing them into a grid and predicting bounding boxes and class probabilities for each cell in a single forward pass, which is what makes it so fast. The presenter discusses the structure of the output vector, which includes class probabilities and bounding box coordinates, and how to handle multiple objects using anchor boxes. Additionally, it covers the non-maximum suppression technique to filter overlapping bounding boxes based on Intersection over Union (IoU) scores. The video sets the stage for a follow-up coding session to implement YOLO in real-world applications.

pairs.video_summary: The video dives into time complexity and algorithm analysis, emphasizing the importance of choosing efficient algorithms for problem-solving. It starts by explaining linear search and binary search techniques for finding elements in a sorted array. Linear search checks each element sequentially, resulting in a time complexity of O(n), while binary search divides the array and eliminates half of the elements with each step, achieving a time complexity of O(log n). The presenter also introduces big O notation as a way to express time complexity, highlighting the significance of optimizing algorithms for scalability and performance. The session wraps up with a promise of exploring more algorithms in future videos.

 in contrast with other approaches , osc employs connectors as first - class constructs . in this way , we leverage reusability and compositionality in the workflow modeling process , specially in the configuration of mechanisms that manage non - functional attributes .

 desse modo , propicia - se uma maior capacidade de reuso e composicionalidade na modelagem de workflows , particularmente nas configuraes dos mecanismos que lidam com atributos no - funcionais .

pairs.video_summary: The video focuses on software architecture, explaining its role as the foundational structure for software development. It discusses the importance of creating a graphical representation before coding, akin to a building blueprint. Key topics include the functionalities of software, database structure and relationships, and the roles of team members in the development process. It also covers various architectural design methods like object-oriented architecture, data flow architecture, and layered architecture, detailing how these frameworks facilitate interaction between users and systems.

in this paper we study automatic recognition of cars of four types : bus , truck , van and small car . for this problem we consider two data driven frameworks : a deep neural network and a support vector machine using sift features . 
 the accuracy of the methods is validated with a database of over 6500 images , and the resulting prediction accuracy is over 97 % . 
 this clearly exceeds the accuracies of earlier studies that use manually engineered feature extraction pipelines .

pairs.video_summary: The video dives into pattern recognition within image analysis, outlining its three main components: object isolation, feature extraction, and classification. It starts with the concept of isolating objects in an image, similar to cleaning a messy room, and emphasizes the importance of accurately identifying and categorizing these objects. The feature extraction process is detailed, highlighting the need for selecting effective features—like number of corners, surface area, and height—to distinguish between classes, such as passenger and racing cars. Finally, it discusses the classification module, which uses these features to label objects, and stresses the significance of choosing independent, discriminatory, and reliable features to optimize classification performance.

pairs.paper_abstract:
we consider the task of pixel - wise semantic segmentation given a small set of labeled training images . among two of the most popular techniques to address this task 
 are random forests ( rf ) and neural networks ( nn ) . 
 the main contribution of this work is to explore the relationship between two special forms of these techniques : stacked rfs and deep convolutional neural networks ( cnn ) . 
 we show that there exists a mapping from stacked rf to deep cnn , and an approximate mapping back . 
 this insight gives two major practical benefits : firstly , deep cnns can be intelligently constructed and initialized , which is crucial when dealing with a limited amount of training data . 
 secondly , it can be utilized to create a new stacked rf with improved performance . 
 furthermore , this mapping yields a new cnn architecture , that is well suited for pixel - wise semantic labeling . 
 we experimentally verify these practical benefits for two different application scenarios in computer vision and biology , where the layout of parts is important : kinect - based body part labeling from depth images , and somite segmentation in microscopy images of developing zebrafish .

pairs.video_summary: The video focuses on how to label your own image dataset for building object detection models, specifically using the YOLOv4 framework. It explains the importance of image annotation, detailing the bounding box labeling technique to identify objects in images. The presenter demonstrates the installation and usage of the LabelImg tool, which allows users to create bounding boxes and save annotations in YOLO format without needing to resize images. The video walks through the installation process on Windows with Anaconda, and shows how to label multiple objects, manage class entries, and ensure that annotation files match image filenames. It also covers editing labels and the normalization of bounding box coordinates.

pairs.paper_abstract:
robust search procedures are a central component in the design of black - box constraint - programming solvers . 
 this paper proposes activity - based search , the idea of using the activity of variables during propagation to guide the search . 
 activity - based search was compared experimentally to impact - based search and the wdeg heuristics . 
 experimental results on a variety of benchmarks show that activity - based search is more robust than other heuristics and may produce significant improvements in performance .

pairs.video_summary: The video dives into search algorithms, starting with the concept of a search node, which includes components like state, parent node, action, path cost, and depth. It introduces the general tree search algorithm, explaining how it uses a fringe to manage unexplored nodes and applies a goal test to determine if a solution has been found. The discussion also touches on different search strategies, such as depth-first and breadth-first search, and emphasizes the importance of effective node selection to manage memory and optimize search efficiency.

pairs.paper_abstract:
in this paper we address the inconsistency of the ekf - based slam algorithm that stems from non - observability of the origin and orientation of the global reference frame . 
 we prove on the non - linear two - dimensional problem with point landmarks observed that this type of inconsistency is remedied using the invariant ekf , a recently introduced variant of the ekf meant to account for the symmetries of the state space . 
 extensive monte - carlo runs illustrate the theoretical results .

pairs.video_summary: The video dives into the functionality of the Frontier device used in robotics, highlighting its embedded computer, multi-camera system, LiDAR, and inertial measurement unit (IMU). It explains how these sensors work together for SLAM (simultaneous localization and mapping), detailing the importance of loop closure to correct accumulated errors in mapping. Additionally, it introduces the factor graph technique for modeling relationships between positions and landmarks, emphasizing how these relationships help optimize the robot's understanding of its environment.

pairs.paper_abstract:
From an environmental standpoint, there are a few crucial aspects of training
a neural network that have a major impact on the quantity of carbon that it
emits. These factors include: the location of the server used for training and
the energy grid that it uses, the length of the training procedure, and even
the make and model of hardware on which the training takes place. In order to
approximate these emissions, we present our Machine Learning Emissions
Calculator, a tool for our community to better understand the environmental
impact of training ML models. We accompany this tool with an explanation of the
factors cited above, as well as concrete actions that individual practitioners
and organizations can take to mitigate their carbon emissions.

pairs.video_summary:
The video dives deep into backpropagation in neural networks, demonstrating its application on both regression and classification datasets. It starts with a regression example, where the presenter manually implements the backpropagation algorithm, explaining each step, including forward propagation, loss calculation using mean squared error, and weight updates via gradient descent. The code is broken down function by function, detailing how to initialize parameters and perform linear forward calculations. 

Then, the same concepts are applied to a classification problem, highlighting changes like using the sigmoid activation function and binary cross-entropy for loss. The presenter also contrasts the manual implementation with Keras, showing how to set initial weights and compare results. The video emphasizes hands-on practice for better understanding and ends with a teaser for the next video, which will cover the theoretical aspects of backpropagation.

pairs.paper_abstract:
flux is a programming method for the design of agents that reason logically about their actions and sensor information in the presence of incomplete knowledge . 
 the core of flux is a system of constraint handling rules , which enables agents to maintain an internal model of their environment by which they control their own behavior . 
 the general action representation formalism of the fluent calculus provides the formal semantics for the constraint solver . 
 flux exhibits excellent computational behavior due to both a carefully restricted expressiveness and the inference paradigm of progression .

pairs.video_summary:
The video dives into the concept of Intelligent Agents in AI, explaining their definition, components, and types. It starts by defining an agent as either software or hardware that processes inputs (called percepts) and produces outputs (actions). The discussion emphasizes the role of sensors, which gather data from the environment, and actuators, which execute actions based on that data. 

Key elements of agent design are introduced, including performance metrics, environmental interactions, and the relationship between inputs and outputs. The presenter highlights the importance of understanding the environment in which the agent operates, noting that it can be dynamic or static, discrete or continuous, and cooperative or competitive. 

Real-world examples, such as self-driving cars and medical diagnosis systems, illustrate how these concepts apply. The video concludes by stressing that the design of an agent must consider its environment and the expected interactions, ultimately shaping its functionality and effectiveness.

we propose a heuristic method that generates a graph for order / degree problem . 
 target graphs of our heuristics have large order ( @xmath0 4000 ) and diameter 3 . 
 we describe the observation of smaller graphs and basic structure of our heuristics . 
 we also explain an evaluation function of each edge for efficient 2-opt local search . using them 
 , we found the best solutions for several graphs .
